newsitem.title: UK: Venezuela could get investment grade this year - DMG.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela could get investment grade this year - DMG.

text.p: Venezuela, which last year finally moved to salvage its deteriorating economy, may get investment grade by the end of 1997 before other major debtor countries in the region, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said on Thursday.
Head of emerging market research Paul Luke compared Venezuela to the turnaround over the past year in Hungary's economy which last month was rated investment grade.
"Provided the Venezuelans persevere with the programme for another year, the results will leave Venezuela with a credit situation, as good as, or even better than, Hungary's.
"We think investors should sell Hungarian bonds and buy Venezuela," he said in a strategy report.
The government has used higher oil income to boost reserves and cut external debt, it has a large current account surplus, the public sector is saving and it has superior debt indicators to Hungary.
There is political support for reform, a major commitment to privatisation and greater openness to foreign investment.
There are signs the political establishment is fed up with failure and is willing to back President Rafael Caldera.

"Caldera prepared the wider population for pain and change, so reactions to gasoline price hikes were muted, in stark contrast to the programme (of his predecessor) which went down with the Venezuelan people like the proverbial maggot risotto."
However, there are question marks over the country's poor performance on inflation and dependence on oil, Luke added.
He noted that Hungarian bonds were very expensive compared to Venezuela's.
National Bank of Hungary 8.8 percent dollar issue of 2002 trades at 96 basis points over U.S. Treasuries while Venezuela's debt conversion bonds (DCBs) have a spread of 413 points.
"The Venezuelan government has money to buy back DCBs big time. The incentive structure to do so is very positive," he added.
